1201.place: Prague and Dresden, on the journey from Vienna to Berlin
1201.event: In the spring of 1789, short of money, Mozart travelled to Prague, Dresden, Leipzig and Berlin hoping to earn from concerts and court appearances. Along the way he wrote affectionate letters to his wife Constanze; from Prague on 10 April he called her his dearest, best little wife, sent kisses to her and their son Karl, and hoped to find a letter from her in Dresden. He carried a small portrait of her, and in a letter of 13 April he described greeting the portrait each day.
1201.explanation: On a hard, uncertain business trip, the mere thought of his wife, kept alive by a portrait and letters, was clearly one of Mozart's chief pleasures.
1201.tie_back: The kural says love is sweeter than wine because it gives joy even when only remembered, and Mozart's playful letters show the delight he took simply in thinking of Constanze while far away.
1201._accuracy_note: Next-best fit: the letters show joy in remembering, but they also show the ache of separation, and the kural's comparison with wine is not reflected in the event.

1202.event_title: John and Abigail Adams sustain their marriage through letters
1202.event: John and Abigail Adams, who married in 1764, exchanged more than 1,100 letters, nearly all now held by the Massachusetts Historical Society. His service in the Continental Congress from 1774 to 1777 and his diplomatic posts in Europe from 1778 to 1784 kept them apart for years at a time, and the letters carried both family news and the business of the Revolution. They continued writing to each other into his presidency, until 1801.
1202.explanation: Through years of separation the couple kept their partnership alive by constantly thinking of and writing to each other.
1202.tie_back: The kural says that when one thinks of the person one loves, the pain of separation does not come, and the Adams letters show long absence softened by steady, loving thought of each other.
1202._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit; the letters show love bridging separation, but they do not show that separation caused no pain at all, as the kural claims.

1203.event_title: The first transatlantic telegraph cable falls silent
1203.event: In August 1858, after several failed attempts, a telegraph cable was completed across the Atlantic between Valentia Island in Ireland and Newfoundland. On 16 August Queen Victoria sent a congratulatory message to President James Buchanan over it. The cable carried 732 messages in about three weeks and then stopped working; a lasting connection came only in 1866.
1203.explanation: The 1858 cable was a thrilling sign that distant people could reach each other, followed almost at once by silence.
1203.tie_back: The kural's heroine feels a sneeze, taken as a sign that someone far away is thinking of her, start and then fade; the 1858 cable was a real-world signal across a great distance that began and then died away.
1203._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural rests on a folk belief about sneezing and a lover's thoughts, and no documented event matches it; the cable is an analogy for a fading sign of contact, not a love story.

1204.event_title: Napoleon's anxious love letters to Josephine from Italy
1204.event: Days after marrying Josephine in March 1796, Napoleon Bonaparte left to command the French Army of Italy. On 30 March he wrote from Nice that he had not spent a day without loving her and thought of her constantly, and he asked why she had addressed him with the formal vous. Through 1796 he begged her to join him and complained that she wrote too rarely; her letters to him have not survived.
1204.explanation: The letters capture a lover sure of his own feelings and openly unsure whether the beloved feels the same.
1204.tie_back: The kural sets 'he is always in my heart' beside the anxious question 'do I have a place in his?', which is the exact tone of Napoleon's letters to Josephine.
1204._accuracy_note: Very close in feeling, though the genders are reversed: here the husband asks whether he has a place in his wife's heart.

1205.event_title: Frida Kahlo paints Diego on My Mind
1205.event: The painter Frida Kahlo married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929; they divorced in late 1939 and remarried in 1940. In 1943 she painted Self-Portrait as Tehuana, also titled Diego on My Mind, a self-portrait whose title names Rivera as the one constantly in her thoughts.
1205.explanation: The painting turns a marriage marked by separation and return into an image of a woman whose mind is occupied by one man.
1205.tie_back: The kural's heroine complains that the man who has shut her out keeps walking into her heart without pause, and Kahlo's Diego on My Mind, painted after he had once divorced her, shows him lodged in her thoughts.
1205._accuracy_note: Good fit for a beloved who occupies the mind, but the couple had remarried by 1943, so the sense of being shut out belongs to their history rather than the moment of the painting.

1206.event_title: Li Qingzhao's Afterword remembers her life with Zhao Mingcheng
1206.event: The poet Li Qingzhao married Zhao Mingcheng in 1101, and together they built a great collection of inscriptions, books and art, living for about ten years in Qingzhou. Zhao fell ill on the way to a new post and died in 1129. Li completed his Record of Metal and Stone and wrote an afterword recalling their life, including their game of guessing where a passage appeared in a book, when she laughed so hard that her tea spilled.
1206.explanation: Widowed, uprooted by war and having lost much of the collection, Li held on to her married life through memory and set it down in one of China's most moving prose pieces.
1206.tie_back: The kural's speaker says she lives only by remembering the days she spent with her husband, and Li Qingzhao's Afterword is that remembering put into writing.
1206._accuracy_note: Strong fit for living on memories of shared days, though here the parting was by death, not by the absence the kural assumes.

1207.event: Søren Kierkegaard became engaged to Regine Olsen on 10 September 1840 and broke the engagement on 12 October 1841, to her great distress. Regine married Johan Frederik Schlegel in 1847, while Kierkegaard never married; he called her his literary life companion and wrote that he was taking her with him into history. His will left her what remained of his estate as a sign that he still regarded the engagement as binding.
1207.explanation: Kierkegaard ended the engagement himself, yet Regine stayed at the centre of his life and work until his death.
1207.tie_back: The kural's heroine says she has never once forgotten her beloved, though even remembering burns; Kierkegaard's lifelong attachment shows a memory that could neither be dropped nor enjoyed in peace.
1207._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for unforgettable, painful memory, but roles are reversed: Kierkegaard was the one who broke off the relationship.

1208.event_title: Johannes Brahms and his lifelong devotion to Clara Schumann
1208.event: The young Johannes Brahms came to the Düsseldorf home of Robert and Clara Schumann in 1853 and was welcomed as a genius. When Robert became gravely ill in 1854 and spent his last two years in an asylum, Brahms helped Clara run the household, care for the children and return to her concert career, and he came to love her. After Robert's death in 1856 they went separate ways but remained lifelong friends through their letters; Brahms never married, and he died within a year of Clara's death in 1896.
1208.explanation: Brahms's long love for Clara was never rejected or resented; it was received as a deep and lasting friendship.
1208.tie_back: The kural's heroine takes comfort that however much she thinks of her beloved, he is never angry with her for it, and Clara accepted Brahms's devotion for forty years without turning it away.
1208._accuracy_note: Next-best: the sources document Brahms's love and the lasting friendship, but Clara's response to his thoughts of her is inferred, and this was not a married couple.

1209.event: On 15 December 1809, in Napoleon's apartments at the Tuileries, his civil marriage to Josephine was formally dissolved; he said he acted for the good of France, since she had not given him an heir. Josephine was so overcome that she could not finish reading her prepared statement and an attendant read the rest. She kept the rank and title of empress and lived at Malmaison until her death in 1814.
1209.explanation: The man who had once written that he could not spend a day without loving her put her aside for reasons of state.
1209.tie_back: The kural's heroine feels her life ebbing as she thinks of the unkindness of the man who once said 'we two are not separate', and Josephine's divorce is a documented case of such a vow of oneness being broken.
1209._accuracy_note: Strong fit for a former vow of unity followed by rejection; the claim that she died of grief is anecdotal and has been left out of the event.

1210.event_title: Su Shi's Mid-Autumn moon poem for his absent brother
1210.event: On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival in 1076, after drinking until dawn, the poet Su Shi wrote a ci lyric to the tune Shuidiao Getou for his younger brother Su Zhe (Ziyou), from whom he had been separated for seven years. The poem speaks to the bright moon and ends with the wish that, though far apart, the two might share its beauty together.
1210.explanation: The poem is still recited at every Mid-Autumn Festival as the classic expression of missing someone under the same moon.
1210.tie_back: The kural's heroine begs the moon not to set so that she may see the one who left yet never left her heart; Su Shi likewise turns to the moon as the link to a loved one far away.
1210._accuracy_note: Next-best: the moon-and-absent-loved-one image matches closely, but the loved one is a brother, not a husband.
